C) Open all Department of the Interior Lands to ORV Use:
This alternative affords to ORV users the broadest range of options to make use of the public lands and would involve the most extensive spectrum of impacts on the non-living features, the plants and animal communities living on those lands, and on other public land users.
Selection of this alternative would result in the following impacts:
There would be more extensive degradation of the surficial resources of the public lands as areas now closed to (or as yet not penetrated by) ORV are designated as open and subsequently used by ORV operators.
If all Interior lands were opened to ORV use, there would be more widespread damage to watersheds, reservoirs, grazing lands, and other such areas which are presently evincing destructive effects of ORV use.
There would be disruption to the maintenance of relationship among the natural communities which are presently reserved as feeding, resting, and breeding grounds for wildlife if ORV operators were given sanctioned entry to all lands administered by the Department.
There, in all likelihood, would be effects of this action which extend well beyond the borders of the public lands to which the action is directly addressed. These effects would relate to conditions which the action causes at the interface of the public lands with the non-public lands.
Existing law prohibits ORV on officially-designated Wilderness Areas or Primitive Areas. Where the Department would open lands so designated to ORV use, it would initiate conflict with laws which established management policies for such areas.
